 SUBSCRIBE Why a routine MLC election matters so much in Bihar today
 The eight-seat polls have become an early stress test for the emerging order, revealing uncertain succession, fragile coalition discipline and a growing challenge from Prashant Kishor's Jan Suraaj
 advertisement Amitabh Srivastava UPDATED: Oct 22, 2026 17:55 IST Edited By: Satyadeep The election to eight legislative council seats in Bihar is unlikely to alter the arithmetic of power in the state. Its political consequences, however, could extend well beyond the Upper House. The contest has emerged as an early test for four men whose ambitions and authority are increasingly intertwined in Bihar’s changing political order.
 Nitish Kumar’s absence from active campaigning raises questions about his continuing hold over the Janata Dal (United). Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary must demonstrate that he can keep the National Democratic Alliance’s disparate constituents in line. Nitish’s son Nishant Kumar faces an early test of his ability to establish political credibility within his father’s party. And Prashant Kishor’s Jan Suraaj is seeking to turn disaffection within the ruling alliance into electoral gains.
 advertisement Read More With JD(U) MLA Anant Singh openly backing Jan Suraaj’s candidate Anuj Singh against his own party’s nominee Neeraj Kumar in the Patna Graduates constituency, the October 23 poll has become more than a contest for council seats. It is a test of who commands loyalty, who can enforce discipline and who can exploit the fractures in Bihar’s new political order.
 The voting on October 23, with counting scheduled for October 27, comes at an awkward moment for the NDA. The BJP has already suffered an unexpected setback in Bankipur, where Jan Suraaj founder Prashant Kishor wrested the seat by 19,324 votes in the August by-election. Now, with the JD(U)’s Mokama legislator openly campaigning against his own party’s nominee in the Patna Graduates constituency, the ruling alliance faces a different kind of challenge: not merely opposition from outside, but dissent from within. 
 advertisement 
 In the graduate constituency, the dispute is as much about personal loyalties and local political rivalries as it is about party discipline. Anant Singh has made little attempt to conceal his position. He has said he will continue to back Anuj, citing what he alleges were Neeraj’s alleged attempts to frame him in the past. Singh claims Neeraj repeatedly tried to ensure his defeat in past assembly elections. Now, he says, it is time to settle the score.
 Singh’s defiance puts the JD(U) leadership in an uncomfortable position: allowing the rebellion to pass without consequence risks weakening the authority of the party’s official candidate, while disciplinary action could expose the limits of its control over a legislator with an independent political following. The episode has also handed Jan Suraaj an opportunity to present itself as a beneficiary of discontent within the ruling alliance.
 The contest has acquired added significance because Nitish, who stepped down as chief minister earlier this year to move to the Rajya Sabha, has not emerged as an active campaigner for the JD(U)’s nominee. For a party whose organisation and electoral appeal have long been closely associated with Nitish’s personal authority, that absence and its effect are conspicuous.
 advertisement It raises a question larger than the fate of a single legislative council seat: can the JD(U) enforce collective discipline when its most influential political figure is no longer directing the government and is not visibly intervening in a local contest? Nitish’s withdrawal from the chief minister’s office may have been orderly, but the transition has not necessarily transferred his authority over the party’s political networks to any one successor.
 That brings Nishant into the picture. Having entered the JD(U)’s political mainstream and taken up a ministerial role, he faces the challenge of demonstrating that his presence can translate into organisational influence. The MLC election is not a direct referendum on his leadership, and its outcome will depend on the dynamics of a limited electorate of registered graduates and teachers. Yet the party’s ability to rally behind its nominee, particularly in a constituency where a sitting MLA is campaigning for the Opposition, will inevitably shape perceptions of Nishant’s emerging political standing.
 The test is not simply whether he can campaign for a candidate or secure a victory. It is whether the JD(U) can develop a leadership structure that functions effectively without relying on Nitish to settle every dispute. A disappointing result for the official nominee would not, by itself, establish that Nishant lacks authority. But it would sharpen questions about who can command loyalty within a party navigating a generational and institutional transition.
 advertisement Choudhary, meanwhile, faces a parallel test. As Bihar’s first BJP chief minister, he must demonstrate that he can manage a coalition in which the JD(U) retains its own political identity, smaller allies have their own ambitions, and local leaders can sometimes act in defiance of the official line. The Patna Graduates contest is therefore not merely an internal JD(U) affair. It is also a test of the chief minister’s capacity to enforce the conventions of coalition politics.
 The difficulty is that the alliance’s public declarations of unity have not necessarily resolved the underlying disputes. Choudhary can convene meetings, appeal for discipline and support the official nominees. But his authority will ultimately be judged by whether the alliance’s leaders and legislators act in accordance with those appeals when local loyalties and political calculations pull them in another direction.
 The eight seats under contest—four graduate and four teacher constituencies—are decided by specialised electorates. Such elections are often shaped by personal outreach, professional networks and the organisational machinery of the competing parties. A rebellion by a sitting MLA or a dissident candidate remaining on the ballot can therefore have consequences beyond its numerical effect on the result. It can expose divisions, unsettle cadres and provide the Opposition with evidence to support its claims that the ruling alliance is less cohesive than it appears.
 advertisement Jan Suraaj, in particular, has an opportunity to convert the disaffection surrounding Anant Singh’s rebellion into a political narrative. Its victory in Bankipur demonstrated that it could defeat the BJP in a constituency long regarded as a party stronghold. The legislative council elections will not necessarily reproduce that result: the electorate is different, the candidates are different, and the political calculations are more localised. But the party can still benefit if the ruling alliance’s internal disagreements undermine its campaign.
 The stakes, then, are less about the composition of the government than about the distribution of authority within Bihar’s political establishment. For Nitish, the contest will test whether his influence remains decisive even when he stays away from the campaign. For Nishant, it will offer an early indication of how far the JD(U) can begin to function under a new generation of leadership. For Choudhary, it will reveal whether the chief minister’s authority extends beyond the formal machinery of government into the competing networks of a coalition.
 A victory for the official NDA candidates would allow the alliance to argue that the early strains have been contained. A poor showing, particularly in a constituency where a sitting JD(U) MLA has openly backed an opponent, would reinforce the impression that the transition from Nitish has left the alliance negotiating a new balance of power.
 The results on October 27 will not determine the government’s survival. They may, however, offer an early indication of who can command loyalty, who can defy the party line and who has the authority to make the alliance act as one.
 In Bihar, that may prove the more consequential verdict.
